title: YOU KNOW THE SIGNS OF THE END TIMES… BUT WHAT IF JESUS IS ASKING WHY YOU IGNORED THE PERSON RIGHT IN FRONT OF YOU?
paragraphs: YOU KNOW THE SIGNS OF THE END TIMES… BUT WHAT IF JESUS IS ASKING WHY YOU IGNORED THE PERSON RIGHT IN FRONT OF YOU?

We can identify the Antichrist, debate the mark of the beast, and recognize the signs of Christ’s return. But what happens when we become experts at predicting tomorrow while neglecting the obedience Jesus commanded today?
Imagine spending your entire life preparing to meet Jesus.

You studied the prophecies. You watched the headlines. You warned people about the last days. You could explain Daniel's seventy weeks, the seven seals of Revelation, the great tribulation, and the coming judgment.
You knew the arguments. You memorized the timelines. You recognized every theory about the Antichrist.
And then, one day, you stand before the Lord.
But the conversation is not what you imagined.
You want to discuss prophecy.
Jesus speaks about obedience.
You want to explain what you discovered about the last days.
Jesus asks what you did with the days He gave you.
You remember the countless hours spent studying the signs of His coming.
And suddenly, you remember the hungry person you walked past.
The family member you refused to forgive.
The neighbor who needed encouragement.
The secret sin you kept postponing repentance over.
The Gospel you were too embarrassed to share.
The wounded believer you condemned instead of helping restore.
And the prayer you kept promising you would pray tomorrow.
Now imagine hearing the words Jesus actually warned about:
"And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?" — Luke 6:46, KJV
Read that again.
Because there is a frightening possibility we need to confront.
What if some Christians are so busy studying when Jesus will return that they are neglecting how Jesus commanded them to live until He returns?
This is not an attack on biblical prophecy.
It is a warning against a faith that knows what Scripture predicts but refuses to practice what Scripture commands.
And before you think about someone else who needs to read this, consider something uncomfortable.
Maybe this message is for us.
Maybe it is for me.
Maybe it is for you.
Because knowing that Jesus is coming back should change the way we live before He arrives.
Not merely the way we interpret the news.
Not merely the videos we watch.
Not merely the arguments we win.
Our actual lives.
Our hearts.
Our relationships.
Our private decisions when nobody is watching.
And if that makes us uncomfortable, perhaps we need to stay with that discomfort long enough to hear what Jesus is saying.
There is something deeply revealing about the final question the disciples asked Jesus before His ascension.
In Acts 1:6, they asked:
"Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?"
They wanted to know the timing.
They wanted to understand what would happen next.
They wanted answers about the kingdom.
And Jesus responded:
"It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power." — Acts 1:7, KJV
Then He immediately redirected their attention.
"But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me..." — Acts 1:8, KJV
Do you see it?
They asked about the schedule.
Jesus spoke about their mission.
They wanted to understand the timing.
Jesus told them they would receive power to become His witnesses.
He did not condemn their interest in God's kingdom. He redirected them from speculation about the Father's timetable toward the responsibility entrusted to them.
The original Greek makes the distinction meaningful.
In Acts 1:7, the words translated "times" and "seasons" are χρόνους (chronous) and καιρούς (kairous).
Chronous refers to periods or durations of time.
Kairous refers to appointed times, seasons, or significant occasions.
Jesus was not inviting His disciples to calculate what the Father had reserved under His own authority.
He was preparing them to testify about Him.
And two thousand years later, the temptation remains.
We want the timeline.
Jesus commands the testimony.
We want to decode every mystery.
Jesus commands us to make disciples.
We want to identify every prophetic symbol.
Jesus commands us to love one another.
We want to know how close we are to the end.
Jesus wants us to remain faithful until the end.
And the tragedy is not that Christians study prophecy.
The tragedy begins when studying prophecy becomes a substitute for following Christ.
Because the book of Revelation was never intended to turn believers into spectators of catastrophe.
It calls the churches to faithfulness, repentance, endurance, and worship.
Revelation 1:3 declares:
"Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy, and keep those things which are written therein: for the time is at hand."
Notice that last part.
Keep those things.
The Greek verb is τηροῦντες (tērountes), from τηρέω (tēreō), meaning to keep, observe, or guard.
The blessing is not presented as a reward for merely solving prophetic mysteries.
It is connected with hearing and keeping God's revealed Word.
That changes everything.
You can study Revelation and still ignore the message of Revelation.
You can recognize the warning to the church of Laodicea while becoming spiritually lukewarm yourself.
You can discuss Babylon's corruption while quietly making compromises with the world.
You can warn others about judgment while refusing to surrender your own pride.
You can talk passionately about the return of the Bridegroom while allowing your love for Him to grow cold.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking possibility of all is this:
You can become so fascinated with the future victory of Jesus that you stop reflecting His character in the present.
Think about the people who followed Jesus during His earthly ministry.
Many expected a Messiah who would immediately overthrow their oppressors and establish visible political power.
They longed for deliverance.
They wanted restoration.
But when Jesus came, He also confronted something much deeper.
Sin.
Self-righteousness.
Hypocrisy.
Spiritual blindness.
The human heart.
He healed the sick.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He touched the untouchable.
He confronted religious pride.
He called people to deny themselves, take up their crosses, and follow Him.
And then He walked toward Calvary.
The King they needed wore a crown of thorns.
The victory they needed came through a cross.
The redemption they needed required His blood.
The Messiah was not simply there to satisfy their expectations.
He came to save His people from their sins.
And that is still where true readiness begins.
Not with the ability to explain every end-time controversy.
But with repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
There is a particular kind of spiritual danger that can hide beneath religious excitement.
It looks like passion.
It sounds like discernment.
It uses Bible verses.
It speaks confidently about deception, judgment, and the last days.
But slowly, almost invisibly, it becomes more interested in exposing darkness than walking in the light.
It becomes more comfortable condemning strangers than confessing personal sin.
It becomes more passionate about proving people wrong than leading them to Christ.
It can spend three hours arguing over a prophetic interpretation and struggle to spend three minutes praying for someone who is hurting.
And nobody notices the change at first.
Not even the person experiencing it.
Because religious activity can make spiritual neglect feel like spiritual maturity.
But Jesus never taught that knowledge alone was the evidence of discipleship.
In John 13:35, He said:
"By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another."
Not by the accuracy of every prediction.
Not by the number of debates won.
Not by the ability to recognize every possible prophetic fulfillment.
By love.
And this love is not a shallow emotion that excuses sin or abandons truth.
Biblical love rejoices in the truth, serves sacrificially, forgives, endures, and seeks another person's good.
It is the kind of love Jesus demonstrated when He washed His disciples' feet.
Including the feet of a man who was about to betray Him.
Pause there.
The Lord who knew what was coming still knelt to serve.
Jesus knew betrayal was approaching.
He knew suffering was near.
He knew the cross awaited Him.
Yet He did not allow His knowledge of what was coming to distract Him from the obedience required in that moment.
And here we are, sometimes using our concern about what is coming as an excuse to neglect what is right in front of us.
The struggling marriage.
The neglected child.
The elderly parent waiting for a visit.
The friend silently battling despair.
The believer who fell into sin and needs truthful, gentle restoration.
The person who has never heard the Gospel clearly explained.
The private habit that has been slowly poisoning our communion with God.
The apology we know we need to make.
The forgiveness we keep withholding.
What if the most urgent thing God is calling you to do today has nothing to do with decoding another headline?
What if it is simply to obey the command you already understand?
Jesus gave a sobering picture in Matthew 24.
While teaching about His return, He described a faithful servant who continued caring for those entrusted to him.
Then He described an evil servant who said in his heart:
"My lord delayeth his coming." — Matthew 24:48, KJV
And what followed?
Neglect.
Abuse.
Self-indulgence.
A servant who lost sight of accountability and began living as though his master would never return.
The point is not that Christians must live in constant panic.
The point is that expectation should produce faithfulness.
The faithful servant was not praised for discovering the exact date of the master's arrival.
He was found doing what his master had entrusted to him.
Jesus said:
"Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing." — Matthew 24:46, KJV
So doing.
Two small words.
A massive spiritual challenge.
Not merely watching.
Not merely discussing.
Not merely calculating.
Doing.
Faithfully serving.
Living obediently.
Being ready.
And perhaps that is why this message cuts so deeply.
Because most of us already know something God has been calling us to do.
We simply keep postponing it.
We tell ourselves we will forgive when the pain becomes easier.
We will repent when the temptation becomes weaker.
We will pray when life becomes quieter.
We will serve when we have more time.
We will share the Gospel when we become more confident.
We will restore the relationship when the other person makes the first move.
Tomorrow.
Next week.
When circumstances improve.
But the problem with tomorrow is that we have never been promised it.
James 4:14 reminds us that our life is like a vapor, appearing briefly and then vanishing.
And Hebrews 3:15 says:
"To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts..."
Today.
Not after the next prophetic conference.
Not after another sensational prediction.
Not after the world becomes more frightening.
Today.
If the Holy Spirit is exposing something in your life right now, do not silence that conviction with another religious distraction.
Bring it to Jesus.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Ask Him for the grace to obey.
Because conviction is not meant to leave us drowning in shame.
It is meant to lead us toward repentance and the mercy of God.
And there is mercy.
More than we deserve.
More than we could ever earn.
Consider Peter.
He had heard Jesus teach about the kingdom.
He had witnessed miracles.
He had confessed that Jesus was the Christ.
He had boldly promised loyalty.
Yet when the pressure came, Peter denied knowing his Lord.
Three times.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The sound of the rooster.
The memory of the warning.
The realization of betrayal.
The eyes of the Savior.
And a man who had spoken so confidently about his devotion suddenly discovered how weak he truly was.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
But his failure was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and called him to care for His sheep.
In John 21, Jesus repeatedly asked Peter whether he loved Him.
And His instructions were strikingly practical.
"Feed my lambs."
"Feed my sheep."
Love for Jesus was to express itself through care for those belonging to Him.
Not merely through dramatic declarations.
Not merely through theological confidence.
Through faithful service.
Peter's story reminds us that even those who fail terribly can be restored by the risen Christ.
That is the Gospel.
Not that we have obeyed perfectly.
But that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for sinners and rose again.
He bore our sins.
He conquered death.
He offers forgiveness and new life to those who repent and believe in Him.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by earning salvation through religious performance.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds these truths together beautifully.
Salvation is God's gift, not the result of our works.
And those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Good works are not the price we pay to purchase salvation.
They are the fruit of a life being transformed by grace.
That distinction matters.
Because this article is not calling you to work harder so Jesus will finally love you.
It is calling you to stop treating His love as though it makes obedience optional.
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace makes restoration possible.
And the Christ who forgives us also calls us to follow Him.
Perhaps you have been spiritually distracted.
Perhaps you know more about the latest prophecy theory than you know about the struggles inside your own home.
Perhaps your social media feed is filled with warnings about the end times, but your prayer life has quietly collapsed.
Perhaps you have become suspicious of everyone, angry at everything, and exhausted by the constant stream of frightening predictions.
Perhaps you genuinely love Jesus but have forgotten what simple, faithful discipleship looks like.
Listen carefully.
You do not have to abandon biblical prophecy to recover biblical obedience.
You need to allow biblical prophecy to accomplish what God intended.
To strengthen your hope.
To deepen your holiness.
To encourage perseverance.
To remind you that evil will not have the final word.
To assure you that Christ will return.
And to move you toward faithful living.
In 2 Peter 3, the apostle speaks of the coming day of the Lord and the future judgment.
But notice the question he asks in verse 11:
"What manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness..."
The Greek expression ποταποὺς ὑπάρχειν ὑμᾶς (potapous hyparchein hymas) asks what sort of people believers ought to be.
Peter's emphasis is not merely on what events will happen.
It is on the kind of lives believers should live in light of those events.
The future calls us to holiness in the present.
And 1 John 3:3 teaches that everyone who has this hope in Christ purifies himself, even as He is pure.
True hope does not encourage spiritual laziness.
It inspires purification.
True expectation does not make love irrelevant.
It makes love urgent.
True confidence in Christ's return does not remove responsibility.
It deepens it.
And we must be careful about another danger.
The temptation to turn every war, earthquake, political development, technological advancement, or global crisis into a confident declaration that we have finally solved the prophetic calendar.
Jesus did tell His followers to remain watchful.
He warned of deception, suffering, and upheaval.
But He also warned against alarm and premature conclusions.
In Matthew 24:6, He said:
"See that ye be not troubled: for all these things must come to pass, but the end is not yet."
And in Matthew 24:36, Jesus taught that no one knows the day and hour of His coming, but the Father.
Christians hold different interpretations of the millennium, tribulation, and sequence of end-time events.
Faithful believers have debated these questions for centuries.
We should study Scripture carefully, compare passages responsibly, and refuse to treat speculation as divine certainty.
But whatever our understanding of the prophetic timeline, we cannot escape the clear commands of Jesus.
Love God.
Love your neighbor.
Repent.
Forgive.
Pray.
Make disciples.
Care for those in need.
Remain faithful.
Abide in Christ.
And be ready.
There is no interpretation of the end times that gives us permission to neglect those commands.
None.
And this becomes even more sobering when we read Matthew 25.
Jesus describes a judgment scene in which the Son of Man separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats.
The passage includes the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the unclothed, the sick, and the imprisoned.
The righteous are surprised by the King's words.
"Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed thee? or thirsty, and gave thee drink?" — Matthew 25:37, KJV
And the King answers:
"Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." — Matthew 25:40, KJV
Christians differ on certain interpretive details of this passage, including the precise identity of "my brethren" in its judgment setting.
But its moral seriousness is unmistakable.
Jesus takes faithfulness, mercy, and our treatment of others seriously.
The passage is not teaching that acts of charity can purchase eternal life.
Rather, it confronts the emptiness of professed allegiance to Christ that bears no evidence of His transforming work.
And that should make every one of us examine our hearts.
Because it is possible to speak endlessly about the coming King while ignoring the commands of the King.
It is possible to defend biblical truth online while treating people cruelly offline.
It is possible to post about judgment while refusing to show mercy.
It is possible to warn strangers about the Antichrist while allowing bitterness to rule our own homes.
It is possible to say, "Come, Lord Jesus," while resisting the Lordship of Jesus in our daily choices.
And that contradiction should grieve us.
Not because Christ has stopped offering grace.
But because His grace is too precious to be treated casually.
There is a woman somewhere reading this who has been praying for her husband to return to God.
A father who is terrified about the spiritual condition of his children.
A young believer who feels overwhelmed by the endless arguments about prophecy.
A person who once loved reading the Bible but now feels trapped in fear after watching too many alarming videos.
A Christian who knows something is wrong in their private life but has learned to hide behind public religious activity.
And perhaps someone who has quietly wondered:
"If Jesus returned today, would He find me faithful?"
That question deserves more than a shallow answer.
But it also deserves more than fear.
Because the answer to spiritual unpreparedness is not frantic religious performance.
It is Jesus Christ.
Run to Him.
Not away from Him.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Surrender what you have been protecting.
Ask Him to renew your love for His Word.
Ask Him to restore your compassion for people.
Ask Him to teach you to watch without becoming fearful, to discern without becoming arrogant, and to speak truth without losing tenderness.
If you have wounded someone, seek reconciliation where possible.
If you have neglected prayer, begin praying again.
If you have been enslaved by a secret sin, bring it into the light and seek faithful help.
If you have stopped serving, ask God where you can begin.
If you have been consumed by end-time anxiety, return to the promises of Christ.
Remember what Jesus said in John 14:3:
"And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also."
Read the tenderness of that promise.
"I will come again."
Not merely to fulfill a chart.
Not merely to complete a sequence of events.
But to receive His people to Himself.
The greatest hope of Christ's return is Christ Himself.
Not the satisfaction of finally proving our interpretation correct.
Not the vindication of winning every argument.
Not the excitement of seeing our predictions unfold.
Jesus.
The One who loved us while we were still sinners.
The One who carried our sins to the cross.
The One whose resurrection secured the hope of eternal life.
The One who intercedes for His people.
The One who will return in glory.
That is whom we are waiting for.
And while we wait, we have been given a mission.
Not to live carelessly.
Not to live terrified.
Not to retreat from the world in endless speculation.
But to live as faithful witnesses of the risen Savior.
Imagine what would happen if Christians devoted as much passion to sharing the Gospel as they devote to debating prophecy.
Imagine if every discussion about the end times ended with someone asking, "Who can I encourage today?"
Imagine if every reminder of Christ's return moved us to forgive more quickly, pray more faithfully, serve more generously, and proclaim Jesus more boldly.
Imagine if the world saw Christians who were not merely skilled at identifying darkness, but unmistakably committed to reflecting the light of Christ.
People who spoke truth with courage.
People who refused to compromise with sin.
People who were quick to repent when wrong.
People who cared for the hurting.
People who remained hopeful in suffering.
People whose lives made others curious about the Savior they professed to follow.
That is not a distraction from biblical prophecy.
That is one of its proper fruits.
And perhaps someone needs to hear this before scrolling to the next article.
You do not need to know the exact date of Christ's return to know what obedience looks like today.
You may not understand every symbol in Daniel.
You may not be able to explain every trumpet in Revelation.
You may still be studying the different Christian interpretations of the tribulation.
But you can pray today.
You can repent today.
You can forgive today.
You can tell someone about Jesus today.
You can open your Bible today.
You can encourage someone who is struggling today.
You can love your family today.
You can surrender your hidden sin today.
You can take the next faithful step today.
And none of those things requires you to solve the prophetic calendar.
It requires you to trust and follow Christ.
That is why this message matters so deeply to us at Gospel Warrior.
Our mission is not simply to produce more Christian content for people to consume.
It is to help people encounter biblical truth, grow in their knowledge of Jesus Christ, confront sin honestly, receive the hope of the Gospel, and mature as disciples.
Because information alone does not transform the heart.
Jesus does.
And we believe that Scripture-centered resources, sound teaching, encouragement, and consistent discipleship can serve that mission.
These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, strengthen their faith, and become better equipped to live for Christ.
And if these messages have encouraged you, challenged you, helped you return to prayer, or reminded you that God's grace has not abandoned you, there is a meaningful way you can help us continue.
It is a voluntary act of generosity that can help sustain and expand this ministry's work.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That is the heart behind our invitation.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But an opportunity to participate willingly in a work you believe is helping others encounter God's Word.
These items are not the reason to follow Jesus.
And whether or not you are able to give financially, you can still help spread the message.
Not merely because sharing increases visibility, but because someone in your circle may be living in fear of the last days while neglecting the hope of the Gospel.
Someone may need to be reminded that Jesus is not calling them to panic, but to faithfulness.
Someone may be studying every prophecy while quietly drifting away from prayer, repentance, and love.
And one simple share could place this biblical reminder before them.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something personal.
Not what you believe the next prophetic event will be.
Not who you think the Antichrist might be.
Not which end-time timeline you defend.
Something much closer to your heart.
What is one act of obedience you know Jesus has been calling you to stop postponing?
Maybe it is repentance.
Maybe forgiveness.
Maybe returning to prayer.
Maybe making peace with someone.
Maybe sharing the Gospel with a person you love.
Maybe turning away from a secret compromise that has been slowly stealing your joy.
You do not have to reveal private details.
But if this message has awakened something in your heart, consider commenting:
Let the comments become a place of prayer, encouragement, honest reflection, and testimony rather than another battlefield of arguments.
Because some of us do not need another debate tonight.
We need to come back to Jesus.
And if you have read this far, perhaps that is the most important truth to carry with you.
The end times are not given to us as an excuse to abandon the present.
The promise of Christ's return is meant to fill our present lives with hope, urgency, holiness, and love.
One day, the last earthly sermon will be preached.
The last opportunity for repentance in this present age will pass.
The promises of God concerning the return of Jesus Christ will be fulfilled.
And every false confidence built on religious appearances will be exposed for what it is.
But those who belong to Christ have a hope that does not rest on their ability to predict the future.
Their hope rests on the crucified and risen Savior.
So study prophecy.
Read Daniel.
Read Revelation.
Learn the Scriptures.
Test every claim carefully.
Reject sensationalism.
Remain watchful.
Hold fast to the promises of God.
But do not neglect the people Jesus has placed in your life.
Do not let your knowledge become a hiding place for disobedience.
Do not confuse prophetic curiosity with spiritual maturity.
And do not allow fear of tomorrow to steal your faithfulness today.
Jesus did not call His disciples merely to know that He would return.
He called them to follow Him until He does.
Perhaps your past is marked by compromise, religious pride, neglected responsibilities, broken promises, or years of spiritual distraction.
Perhaps you have spent so long watching for the signs that you have stopped listening to the Shepherd.
But your story does not have to end there.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is restoration for the repentant.
There is grace for the weary.
There is a new beginning for the one who turns to Jesus in faith.
Your failures do not have to write the final sentence of your life.
Because the Savior who restored Peter still calls sinners to repentance, faith, and a transformed life.
And when the world becomes loud with predictions, arguments, fear, and uncertainty, remember the simplicity of His call:
"Follow me." — John 21:19, KJV
Not tomorrow.
Not when you have figured everything out.
Today.
Do not become so consumed with watching the sky for His return that you forget to follow His footsteps on the ground.
